definition: A network card with its own processor cores and accelerators that runs networking, storage and security software so the server's main CPU does not have to.
NVIDIA's name for a network card dedicated to moving data between GPUs in the back-end network (ConnectX-8/9 and BlueField-3 SuperNIC), typically one per GPU.
A network card that offloads some packet processing (for example virtual switching or encryption) from the CPU; a DPU is a SmartNIC with general-purpose cores.
A way for one computer to read or write another computer's memory over the network without involving either CPU, cutting latency and CPU load.
The standard for running RDMA over Ethernet instead of InfiniBand; it traditionally needs a loss-free network to perform well.
NVIDIA's software development kit and runtime for BlueField DPUs and SuperNICs, the DPU counterpart of CUDA.
An open Ethernet transport for AI and HPC defined by the Ultra Ethernet Consortium (spec 1.0, June 2025), with multipath packet spraying, packet trimming and new congestion control.
AWS's network interface for HPC and AI instances, built on Nitro cards and the SRD transport rather than InfiniBand or standard RoCE.
AWS's own transport protocol, used by EFA, that sprays packets across many network paths and recovers losses in hardware.
AWS's family of in-house offload cards and hypervisor that run EC2 networking, storage, management and security off the host CPU; it grew out of the 2015 Annapurna Labs acquisition.
Intel's (and Google's) term for a DPU: a programmable network device that runs cloud infrastructure functions off the host CPU.
A language for programming how a network chip parses and forwards packets, used by AMD Pensando and Intel IPU pipelines.
Sending the packets of one flow over many network paths at once to avoid hot spots; the receiving NIC puts them back in order.
Google's hardware-assisted network transport for data-center Ethernet, contributed to the Open Compute Project in 2023; Intel's IPU E2000 was its first hardware platform.
Running code and data inside a hardware-protected enclave (trusted execution environment) so that even the cloud operator cannot read them; NVIDIA supports it on GPUs from Hopper onwards.
The ordinary data-center network that connects servers to storage, users and the internet, as opposed to the GPU-to-GPU back-end network.
The dedicated scale-out network that links GPUs across servers for training and inference collectives; typically one NIC per GPU.
NVIDIA technology that moves data directly between storage (local NVMe or over the network) and GPU memory, bypassing a copy through CPU memory.

A storage tier for AI inference that keeps KV caches (the model's working memory of a conversation) on fast flash near the GPUs so they can be reloaded instead of recomputed; NVIDIA's BlueField-4 STX targets it.
Chips a company designs for its own use and does not sell (for example AWS Nitro or Microsoft's Azure Boost DPU), as opposed to merchant silicon.
The software layer that splits one physical server into many virtual machines; offloading it to a DPU or Nitro card frees host CPU cores and hardens isolation.
